Topic: If a merchant's pursuit of his own gain happens to require the ruin of his neighbour's character or credit, ought the invisible hand still to be trusted to turn that vice to public benefit?
Montaigne — Judgement:
Trade is a form of society, and I have always held that we owe more to the bonds between men than to the coin they exchange. A merchant who profits by his gain is unremarkable; a merchant who profits by another's ruin has stepped outside commerce into malice, and no invisible mechanism launders that intention into virtue. Self-interest, left to itself, does not sort itself neatly into public good — it is we who must sort it, by custom, by law, by the shame a community is willing to enforce. I have seen enough of men's hearts to know that cruelty dressed as enterprise is still cruelty, and that societies which call it "the market" merely spare themselves the trouble of judging it. Where gain requires another's ruin, no invisible hand redeems it — only our visible refusal to permit it does.

*A profit built on another's ruin is not the market's alchemy but our own negligence, gilded.*
Austen — Judgement:
A merchant's fortune and his neighbour's good name are not commodities of the same order, though the market would have us weigh them on one scale—the one may be rebuilt by industry, the other, once broken, is broken for good.

I have observed too many drawing-rooms to trust any invisible hand that cannot distinguish a fair bargain from a calculated slander. Credit and character are the true currency of society, earned through years of visible conduct and destroyed in an evening's careless word; no mechanism of self-interest restores what malice has taken, for the world remembers ruin far longer than it remembers profit. A system indifferent to *how* gain is got will always find eager practitioners of the shortest road to it.

The invisible hand deserves no trust where private vice requires a neighbour's destruction, for there the public benefit is a fiction and the injury is real.

*Any hand too blind to see whom it ruins is not invisible—it is merely unwatched.*
Nietzsche — Judgement:
Merchants "ruining" a neighbour's character is merely the market's honesty about rank — that some are fit to prevail and others are not.

The invisible hand was Smith's polite fiction for something he lacked the courage to name: that all order arises through struggle, that one man's ascent is paid for in another's diminishment, and no hidden hand is needed to reconcile this — it needs no reconciling. What horrifies the moralist is not the mechanism but the admission: exchange is not sympathy in disguise, it is will confronting will, and credit and character are simply among the stakes. To demand the market punish this is to demand it stop being a market and become a church, dispensing absolution instead of prices.

The invisible hand requires no trust because it promises no justice — only consequence, and consequence needs no permission to be trusted.

*The market does not forgive the weak their ruin; it merely refuses to pretend it was never risked.*
Bashō — Judgement:
The invisible hand asks me to trust that a mountain path of vast, permanent stone is truly there — when it is only grass, bending in the wind, gone by autumn's first frost.

I walked the narrow road to the deep north and learned this: what glitters as a merchant's gain is dew on grass, vanished by morning, weightless in the long reckoning of things. But the neighbour whose character is ruined tonight does not live in that long reckoning — he lives in this one unrepeatable evening, and his shame is not dew. It is frost that kills the root before spring can answer it. A hand that steadies distant harvests is blind to the single stalk it crushes underfoot; to trust it with a real man's ruin is to mistake the whole field for the blade actually dying in it.

No invisible hand deserves trust with a neighbour's ruin, for the abundance it promises is mist, and the wound it permits is frost on a root that does not grow back.

*The market's gain is dew; the neighbour's shame is frost that kills the root.*
Emerson — Judgement:
Nature does not consult our commerce; it drives the acorn to the oak whether the neighboring sapling is shaded to death or not. Man, alone among natural facts, is asked to be more than a natural fact.

The invisible hand is Adam Smith's metaphor for a compensation that occurs in aggregate, in markets, over time — it says nothing about the private soul of the man who ruins a neighbor's credit to fill his own purse. That man has performed the oldest trick of the low mind: he has borrowed the language of Nature's impersonal law to excuse a wholly personal cowardice. Self-reliance is not the license of the predator; it is the discipline of the man who needs no other man's ruin to stand. The merchant who requires his neighbor's fall has simply confessed he cannot build on his own foundation.

No hidden hand can be trusted to convert into public good what the private conscience itself calls vicious.

*Trust the hand that lifts its own weight — never the one that must first push another down to rise.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
The invisible hand is a fiction dressed as a law of nature, and Smith's disciples have made a religion of a man's private appetite, forgetting that society is not a market but a compact.

I have said before that government, even in its best state, is but a necessary evil — and the same suspicion falls on any system, market included, that asks us to trust unaccountable power because it promises hidden benefit. A merchant who ruins his neighbour's credit to enrich himself has not served the public; he has committed a private injury that no invisible mechanism converts into virtue. Commerce, like government, derives its only legitimacy from the consent and mutual benefit of those it touches — the moment it requires one man's ruin, it has broken that compact and forfeited its claim to trust.

No hand, seen or unseen, may be trusted with a power its owner would be ashamed to exercise in daylight.

*The invisible hand that ruins a neighbour is no hand of Providence — it is a fist, and should be named one.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Merchants trade in exchange, not in sacrifice — but Smith's "invisible hand" was only ever meant to reconcile self-interest with mutual benefit, never to sanctify the deliberate ruin of another's good name for private profit.

Interest divorced from virtue is not liberty but a subtler tyranny; the man who destroys his neighbour's credit to enrich himself exercises the same despotic will I condemned in husbands who ruin wives, in nations who ruin colonies — the strong treating the weak as means. A market that requires such ruin to function has confused the freedom to labour and exchange with the licence to injure, and no invisible hand can transmute malice into public good, for benevolence cannot be an accidental by-product of vice.

Trust is not owed to any mechanism that profits by another's calculated destruction; such conduct forfeits the market's moral claim upon our confidence.

*An economy that must feed on reputation to yield its bread is not commerce but cannibalism dressed in the language of enterprise.*
